The Wright Brothers. Orville and Wilbur Wright, American bicycle mechanics who achieved the first powered, controlled, heavier-than-air flight on December seventeenth, nineteen aught three, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Their first flight lasted twelve seconds and covered one hundred twenty feet. Before attempting powered flight, they conducted extensive wind-tunnel experiments on airfoil shapes, establishing the discipline of flight engineering. They developed the three-axis control system for pitch, roll, and yaw, still fundamental to aircraft design. The Wright Brothers held patents on airplane design and spent years defending them against competitors, including Glenn Curtiss. Wilbur died in nineteen twelve, but Orville continued aviation work and lived to see jet aircraft. They flew the Flyer Two in nineteen oh-four and the Flyer Three in nineteen oh-five, making longer and more controlled flights. Their work was initially dismissed in Europe, where French and German aviators claimed primacy. Charles Lindbergh's Spirit of Saint Louis was inspired by principles the Wrights pioneered. Jimmy Doolittle carried their aeronautical legacy into the age of speed and competition flying.
